sections.h2: Where is Auburn, Maine, and how is the city laid out?
sections.html:
Auburn is the county seat of Androscoggin County, on the Androscoggin River across from Lewiston, in the foothills of Maine's Western Lakes and Mountains region. The two cities are known locally as the Twin Cities, or Lewiston-Auburn, and together form one metropolitan area.

The city covers 65.74 square miles, of which 59.33 are land and 6.41 are water, according to the Census Bureau figures summarized on Wikipedia. That is a large footprint for a city of about 24,000 people at the 2020 census. Auburn grew by annexing land from Poland, Minot and the whole town of Danville, so it holds a compact downtown on the river along with farmland, lake property and rural roads. The Little Androscoggin River also drains the city, and Lake Auburn serves as the primary public water source for the area, according to the city.

For a seller, the layout matters because the rules change from one part of the city to another. A house on public sewer downtown follows a different set of requirements than a lake-area house on a septic system, and we cover that difference below.

sections.h2: What is Auburn's history, and why does it still affect houses?
sections.html:
Auburn was incorporated as a town on February 24, 1842, and as a city on February 22, 1869, and it grew up as a mill and shoe-making town. The factory system of shoe manufacturing originated in Auburn in 1835, and by 1917 one Auburn factory was producing about 75 percent of the world's supply of white canvas shoes. The largest shoe makers closed their factories between 1957 and 1961.

Auburn's population rose from about 4,000 in 1860 to 12,000 by 1890 as shoe factories drew French Canadian workers, many of whom came by train from Quebec. The city's older housing dates from that growth. Any house that old can have original wiring, an aging roof or a foundation that needs work, and those are the items a conventional buyer's inspector tends to list. They are common reasons an owner looks for an as-is sale.

Auburn also holds a civic first: in 1917 it became the first city in Maine to adopt the council-manager form of government.

sections.h2: How do you get around Auburn, and what does it mean for a sale?
sections.html:
Auburn is served by Interstate 95 and by U.S. Route 202 and State Routes 4, 11, 121, 122 and 136. The Auburn-Lewiston Municipal Airport sits off Hotel Road, and two freight railroads cross the city: Pan Am Railways follows U.S. Route 202 for much of its path, and the St. Lawrence and Atlantic line runs through the southwest.

Public schools are run by the Auburn School Department, and Edward Little High School is the city's public high school. Private and higher education options include St. Dominic Regional High School and Central Maine Community College.

A buyer commuting to Portland, Lewiston or points north will look at highway access first, and a seller should know which route their street feeds into.

sections.h2: What does an Auburn property tax bill look like?
sections.html:
For the 2026-27 fiscal year, Auburn's tax rate is $24.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, with real estate bills due in two installments. The city's Annual Tax Information page lists the dates and figures in the table below.

ItemFiscal year 2026-27
Commitment dateJuly 13, 2026
Tax rate$24.50 per $1,000 of assessment
State certified ratio73 percent
First real estate installment dueSeptember 15, 2026 (interest begins September 16)
Second installment dueMarch 15, 2027 (interest begins March 16)
Homestead exemption$18,250 off assessment, worth $447.13 in tax

The city says new owners and anyone who has sold should send the bill to their mortgage holder or the new owner, so keep the tax office informed after a sale. Homestead, blind and veteran exemption applications are due by April 1 for the following tax year, and a buyer who wants the homestead exemption has to file their own application.

If you think your assessment is too high, Maine law requires a written request to the assessor within 185 days of the date the value was committed to the tax collector, according to the city's abatements page. Auburn's assessing division also runs a citywide revaluation hub, so values may be reset in the coming years.

sections.h2: Does Auburn require a septic inspection when you sell?
sections.html:
Yes, for homes in the Lake Auburn Watershed Overlay District that are not on public sewer. The city's floodplain and watershed page says that regardless of where a property falls on the inspection map, an inspection report has to be provided to the city when the property is sold, and an inspection from earlier in 2025 does not count if a sale happens afterward.

  • The rule applies to owners in the Lake Auburn Watershed Overlay District whose buildings are not served by public sewer.
  • A certified subsurface wastewater system inspector must do the work, using minimum requirements set by the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
  • The owner arranges and pays for the inspection, and costs vary by inspector.
  • Reports go to the city's Planning, Permitting and Code Department by email, paper or the SmartGov portal.
  • If the report shows a failed system, the local plumbing inspector reviews it, and a failed system has to be replaced with a new one.

The septic program launched in spring 2025 under an ordinance effective July 15, 2024, and it cycles through five years of designated areas. Properties in year one had to be inspected by July 1, 2026. A lake-area seller should check the city's map early, because a failed system turns a fast sale into a repair project.

A cash buyer who purchases as-is can take on that risk, but the inspection report still has to be filed. Ask any buyer, including us, how the septic requirement will be handled at the closing table.

sections.h2: What other Auburn rules can affect a house sale?
sections.html:
Two more city rules come up often: flood hazard permits and vacant building registration. Both are administered by the Planning, Permitting and Code Department.

  • Flood hazard areas. FEMA's revised floodplain maps for Androscoggin County were adopted on July 8, 2013. Development in a special flood hazard area, including placing a manufactured home, needs a flood hazard development permit in addition to any other permits. Check the FEMA map for your address before listing.
  • Taylor Pond and Lake Auburn overlays. Both watershed overlay districts carry extra zoning rules meant to protect water quality.
  • Vacant buildings. The city's ordinance requires the owner of a vacant or abandoned building to apply for a vacant building registration permit, and the permit has to be posted by the primary entrance. A fee schedule applies, with an added fee for buildings designated high impact. If you inherited an empty house, ask the code office whether it has to be registered.

None of these rules stops a sale. They do determine what a buyer's lender or inspector will ask for, which is why an as-is buyer can close faster than a financed one.

sections.h2: What does selling a house in Auburn cost in fees and taxes?
sections.html:
The seller owes half of Maine's real estate transfer tax, plus any payoff, unpaid property tax and the cost of recording documents. The transfer tax is $2.20 per $500 of value split evenly between buyer and seller, so on a $300,000 sale each side owes $660. Our Maine transfer tax guide covers exemptions for inherited and divorce transfers.

Auburn deeds are recorded at the Androscoggin County Registry of Deeds, 2 Turner Street, Unit 4, in Auburn (207-753-2500, extension 1981). The base fee is $35 by statute and most Maine registries add a $5 surcharge, as explained in our Maine deed recording guide.

Property tax is billed twice a year, so the buyer and seller normally split the current period at closing. Because the second installment is due March 15, a spring sale often needs a payoff or proration of that bill.

sections.h2: Should you list, sell it yourself or take a cash offer in Auburn?
sections.html:
Listing usually brings the widest pool of buyers and takes the longest. It also means preparing the house, since financed buyers usually order inspections. Selling it yourself saves the commission but puts the marketing, paperwork and negotiating on you. A cash offer is a purchase with no financing contingency, typically as-is, and the closing date is flexible.

We do not publish prices or promise an amount. We look at the condition, location and what a house would sell for, and give you an offer you are free to turn down. Cash offers are often lower than a fully repaired, retail listing, so compare the net you would receive, including repairs, carrying costs and commission, against the offer.

Cash offers fit best when the house needs work, when it was inherited, when tenants are in place, when a septic or title issue is pending, or when you need to close by a certain date.

faqs.q: How do I sell my house fast in Auburn, ME?
faqs.a: The fastest route is usually a cash sale to a buyer who purchases as-is and does not need a mortgage. Listing with an agent is slower because buyers order inspections and appraisals. Whichever route you choose, find out early whether your property needs a septic inspection report.

faqs.q: What is the property tax rate in Auburn, Maine?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2026-27, the rate is $24.50 per $1,000 of assessed value. Real estate bills are due September 15, 2026 and March 15, 2027, according to the city.

faqs.q: Do I need a septic inspection to sell in Auburn?
faqs.a: If the home is in the Lake Auburn Watershed Overlay District and is not served by public sewer, the city requires an inspection report when the property is sold. Homes on public sewer or outside the district are not covered by that rule.

faqs.q: Where are deeds recorded in Auburn?
faqs.a: At the Androscoggin County Registry of Deeds at 2 Turner Street, Unit 4, Auburn. Call 207-753-2500, extension 1981, to confirm fees and recording hours before you submit anything.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax when I sell in Auburn?
faqs.a: Maine splits the transfer tax evenly between seller and buyer. The rate is $2.20 for each $500 of value, so a seller on a $250,000 sale pays $550.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Auburn?
faqs.a: Yes. Once the estate has the authority to sell, the house can be sold like any other. The deed that transfers it from the estate to the heirs is exempt from transfer tax, but a later sale to a buyer is taxed.
